entities.name: John de la Pole, 1st Earl of Lincoln
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John de la Pole, 1st Earl of Lincoln, emerged as a pivotal, albeit ultimately tragic, figure in the final, desperate acts of the Wars of the Roses, serving as the designated heir to Richard III and a central player in the Yorkist counter-reformation against the nascent Tudor dynasty. Born the eldest son of John de la Pole, 2nd Duke of Suffolk, and Elizabeth of York, sister to Kings Edward IV and Richard III, Lincoln represented a direct, legitimate claim to the English throne through his royal mother, placing him at the heart of the dynastic struggles that convulsed England in the late 15th century. His brief but intense period of influence spanned from 1485 to 1487, during which he embodied the last significant threat to Henry VII's consolidation of power, leading a rebellion that sought to restore the House of York.

Following Richard III's defeat and death at the Battle of Bosworth Field in August 1485, Henry Tudor ascended as King Henry VII, initiating the Tudor era. Lincoln, despite initially swearing fealty to Henry, harbored strong Yorkist loyalties and quickly became a focal point for discontent. In 1487, he fled England for Mechelen, Burgundy, joining forces with Margaret of York, Duchess of Burgundy, who provided financial and military support. There, he orchestrated the Lambert Simnel rebellion, a daring attempt to install a pretender, Simnel, as Edward Plantagenet, Earl of Warwick, a surviving Yorkist prince. Lincoln himself was widely believed to be the true power behind Simnel, effectively asserting his own claim through the boy. Leading an army of Irish mercenaries and German landsknechts, he invaded England in June 1487, culminating in the decisive Battle of Stoke Field near Newark-on-Trent.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: John de la Pole's death at the Battle of Stoke Field in 1487 effectively extinguished the last viable Yorkist claim to the English throne, cementing Henry VII's nascent Tudor dynasty and bringing a decisive end to the Wars of the Roses. His rebellion, though failed, represented a critical test for the new monarchy, whose successful suppression ensured decades of relative dynastic stability.
